summary:
Same-sex conduct between men was decriminalised in Barbados in December 2022, on the outcome of a constitutional challenge filed in June 2018 with trans activist Alexa Hoffmann as claimant, supported by the Canadian HIV/AIDS Legal Network and the University of Toronto's international human-rights programme. A High Court ruling on sodomy, published in May 2023, found discrimination based on sexual orientation unconstitutional.

Barbados does not screen or protect LGBT travellers as a distinct category, and the state has questioned the legitimacy of LGBT migration. In 2011 the government said it was investigating claims that gay Barbadians were seeking refugee status in Canada. In 2016 Foreign Minister Maxine McClean expressed concern that such applications were an attempt to abuse the Canadian refugee system, noting that two of nine Canadian applications had been denied, and a Guyanese newspaper reported over 300 LGBT members in Barbados seeking asylum in Canada, the United Kingdom and the United States; UGLAAB said it would investigate the same allegations.

Employment protection stops short of trans people. The Employment (Prevention of Discrimination) Act, 2020, passed by Parliament in August 2020, bars employment discrimination on grounds including sex, sexual orientation and domestic partnership status, but trans activist Alexa D.V. Hoffmann argues that it excludes trans workers because gender identity and gender expression are not listed as protected grounds.

Violence against trans people has produced a documented impunity outcome. In February 2018 Hoffmann was attacked with a meat cleaver by Brandon Coward and suffered serious injuries including to her throat. Coward was convicted in April 2019 and ordered to pay Hoffmann BDS$460 (US$230) or serve three months in prison; no jail time was imposed. The most recent documented case in this record is from 2018, with sentencing in 2019; no later instance is documented.

No same-sex relationship or union is recognised in Barbados. In June 2016 the government ruled out changing the law to allow same-sex marriage, and in September 2020 it announced only a plan to recognise "some form" of civil union followed by a referendum on gay marriage. Critics said the civil union proposal was unnecessarily vague and that the referendum was likely to fail, and as of the source's account neither had been enacted.

Entry rules for the "Welcome Stamp" remote-work visa introduced in July 2020 initially allowed foreign workers to bring only an opposite-sex spouse, and were changed to permit same-sex spouses.

Regional protection machinery is unresolved in the record. In 2018 activists filed a case with the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights challenging the Sexual Offences Act (Ch.154, ss.9 and 12), and the Commission gave the government three months to respond in late July 2019; failure to repeal could send the matter to the Inter-American Court of Human Rights for a binding decision. The record does not resolve what became of that case after the December 2022 decriminalisation.
tangentialFactors:
Official and religious hostility toward LGBT people runs through the record. In 2016 Attorney General Adriel Brathwaite stated that Barbados would not change the law to allow same-sex marriage, and following UK Prime Minister David Cameron's 2011 Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting aid warning about sodomy laws he publicly said Barbados would not be dictated to by the United Kingdom. A government minister warned that external forces were trying to impose same-sex marriage, prompting Human Rights Watch to call the response a cheap political trick because its report did not mention same-sex marriage.

Fundamentalist groups including the New Testament Church have claimed sexual orientation is chosen and argued that discrimination against LGBT people should be encouraged, and human rights activists say that arriving American evangelical ministers have spread homophobic rhetoric more widely. The Barbados Nation newspaper's informal comment line drew opposition to a proposed gay tourism package. The Anglican Bishop of Barbados and the Catholic Church are recorded as opposing the buggery law while respecting LGBT rights, and Prime Minister Mia Mottley, elected in May 2018, is reported as pro-LGBT.

The Human Dignity Trust documents constitutional challenges to sodomy laws across the Eastern Caribbean, and Barbados decriminalised same-sex conduct in December 2022 through such a challenge, placing it alongside neighbouring jurisdictions that have moved the same way.
localsOnly:
Family formation is restricted for same-sex couples in Barbados: they are unable to legally adopt, surrogacy is illegal although not explicitly prohibited or regulated by law, and same-sex couples are not recognised as families. The only parenting-related service identified in the record is the Barbados Fertility Centre, which offers IVF and artificial insemination to lesbian couples.

An August 2020 commentary reported trans Barbadians being fired or denied jobs for "dressing wrong", under an employment act whose listed protected grounds do not include gender identity or gender expression.

Barbados Gays, Lesbians and All-Sexuals Against Discrimination (BGLAD), founded in 2013 by Donnya Piggott and Ro-Ann Mohammed, was set up to create an education mechanism and open public dialogue for the LGBT community. Pride events have served an awareness-raising function, with a first small event in November 2017 and a parade of about 120 people on Rihanna Drive, Bridgetown, in July 2018. A second Trans Day of Remembrance vigil was held in November 2018 with NOW, a local ally and veteran trans advocates, and Alexa Hoffmann has given a first-person account of visibility and danger on the island.
outOfScopeNotes:
Identity-document processes and legal gender recognition for trans Barbadians are not covered by any source in this record; no procedure, eligibility test or waiting period is documented, and the absence of findings should not be read as either availability or refusal.

No findings appear on access to transition-related healthcare, mental health or specialist care. The only health-related provisions identified are the Barbados Fertility Centre's IVF and artificial insemination for lesbian couples, the illegal status of surrogacy, and UGLAAB's work on AIDS.

No findings appear on trans-specific custody, parental rights or family law outcomes, on the treatment of LGBT minors, on detention of unaccompanied youth, or on school-based anti-bullying and gender-affirming education. The only youth-adjacent legal detail in the record is that under the former Section 12 of the Sexual Offences Act, "serious indecency" carried a maximum penalty of ten years in prison where the act was committed on or towards a person aged 16 or older; whether that provision remains in force is unresolved in the sources.

No trans-specific violence or killing rate is available for Barbados, and the record supplies no general homicide rate against which one could be measured. The violence finding rests on individual documented incidents, the most recent of which dates from 2018 with sentencing in 2019.

Two legal questions remain unresolved in the record: the status of the 2018 Inter-American Commission on Human Rights case after the December 2022 decriminalisation, and whether the September 2020 plan for a civil union or the accompanying referendum was ever enacted. The sources describe neither as passed at the time of writing and nothing later is sourced.
